George Balanchine was a Russian-American choreographer who revolutionized ballet through speed, athleticism, and abstract movement, casting off the narrative constraints of classical ballet to create a purely American neoclassical style. Born in St. Petersburg in nineteen four as Giorgi Balanchivadze, he studied at the Imperial Ballet Academy and danced with the Ballets Russes under Sergei Diaghilev. He pioneered neoclassical ballet, stripping away elaborate sets and costumes to focus on the human body and the music's architecture. In nineteen forty-eight, he co-founded New York City Ballet with Lincoln Kirstein, elevating it to a world-class company despite chronic underfunding. He collaborated intensively with composer Igor Stravinsky, creating masterworks including Apollo, Serenade, and The Nutcracker, which he reimagined as a one-act ballet. He defined the Balanchine body—long, lean, high-extension lines with speed of footwork and emphasis on the upper spine and neck in a distinctly American aesthetic. He created abstract ballets with no plot, breaking the nineteenth-century mold of pantomime-heavy storytelling; his Agon, created in nineteen fifty-seven, remains among the most innovative ballets ever made. He worked with hundreds of dancers including Suzanne Farrell, his eye for talent and ability to extract new movement vocabularies from dancers shaping an entire generation.
